scenes.title: hook (same aim, one player or eighteen)

voiceover.text: So, how do you start designing a training session? Two coaches have sixty minutes and the same goal: improve the ability to repeat hard efforts with short recovery. One coaches a single junior tennis player. The other coaches eighteen netballers of mixed fitness. The physiology is identical. Write down three things about the session that must still be designed differently, and why. Then decide which of your three is about safety, not just convenience.

scenes.title: the aim comes first, and it's goal specific

voiceover.text: A session is planned in an order: aim, safety, warm-up, the main work, and cool-down. The aim comes first, and the syllabus says it should be goal specific. That means it states what the session should change, so you can check afterwards whether it worked. Compare three tries. "Do some fitness work" is an activity, not an aim. "Improve fitness" is a direction, but any session would satisfy it. Now this: improve the ability to repeat five-second sprints with fifteen seconds' recovery, measured as the drop-off across ten repetitions. That fixes the quality trained, the work-to-rest structure, the volume and the measure. And it decides everything after it. If you can't say what evidence would show it worked, you don't have an aim yet, only an activity.

scenes.title: one athlete's aim, a squad's aim

voiceover.text: The same aim plays out differently in the two settings. For the tennis player, it's their own goal, from their own testing and their own season, so it can be very narrow: one weakness, the whole hour. For the netball squad, it's a team goal, chosen because it serves how the team plays, and it has to be worth doing for most of the eighteen. Individual needs are met inside it by differentiation: the same drill with different distances, loads, repetitions or roles. And evaluation differs too. One athlete is compared with their own past results, so small changes count. A squad needs team measures plus a sample of individuals, because an average can hide both the player who improved most and the one who barely trained.

scenes.title: health and safety: the loop, environment and facilities

voiceover.text: Safety earns marks when it's a process. Identify the hazards, judge how likely and how serious each one is, control it, then check the control is still there on the day. Remember duty of care from screening: reasonable steps against harm you could foresee. Five kinds of hazard. Environment: heat, storms, poor light, a wet surface, and a squad of eighteen needs more fluid stations.

scenes.title: health and safety: athlete, activity and emergencies

voiceover.text: The athlete: injury, illness, fatigue, with eighteen histories to track instead of one. The activity: one athlete can be watched constantly, a squad only on and off, so drills must be safe when unwatched. And emergencies. When the coach kneels beside an injured player, seventeen others are unsupervised, so the plan must say what they do. And telling athletes to be careful isn't a control.

scenes.title: warm-up and cool-down, in the two settings

voiceover.text: Earlier you saw what a warm-up and cool-down do: a general warm-up raises temperature and blood flow, a specific one rehearses the session's movements, and a cool-down returns the body gradually towards rest. What changes here is how they're delivered. For one athlete, the warm-up can be built around their own history and the exact session ahead. For a squad, there's a common core, plus extra work for anyone returning from injury. A squad warm-up also takes longer, because organising eighteen people takes time. And it has to be simple enough to do correctly without the coach watching. The cool-down differs too. One athlete can extend it into flexibility or rehab work. For a squad, it's often the only reliable moment for whole-team feedback and plans for next session.

scenes.title: three causes, and what doesn't change

voiceover.text: So here's how to answer a compare question. Don't write one paragraph per sport. Name the aspect, place each setting on it, and give the reason. Every difference you've seen comes from one of three causes: eighteen sets of needs instead of one, the coach's attention divided instead of whole, and a shared clock and shared space. Then say what's the same, because that earns marks too. The physiology doesn't change with squad size. The same energy system needs the same work-to-rest structure. Both aims must be goal specific, and every hazard category applies to both. One last trap. Tennis and netball also differ because of the court and the rules. Those are sport differences. The real test is whether the difference would still exist between singles and doubles.
Two things to remember. If you can't evaluate it, it's an activity, not an aim. And every difference comes from many needs, divided attention, or a shared clock and space.

Two exam questions. First. A coach's plan says "Endurance session." Another says "Work on the athletes' weaknesses." Rewrite each as a goal-specific aim, and name the one measure you'd use to judge it. Pause here to answer.

For A, something like: hold eighty per cent of maximum heart rate for forty minutes of continuous running, measured by heart rate at a fixed pace next week. For B, name the weakness from testing, say a slow first step, and the drill, measured by a ten-metre sprint time. The classic mistake is just adding detail about the activity.

Second. One sixty-minute session, one aim: repeat six-second maximal efforts with twenty-four seconds' recovery. Plan it for a single seventeen-year-old sprint kayaker, and for a squad of eighteen mixed-ability rugby league players. Compare two aspects of safety or warm-up, giving the cause of each difference, and state one thing that stays the same. Pause here to answer.

Safety: the kayaker can be watched constantly near the water, while the squad needs drills safe when unwatched and spacing against collisions, because attention is divided. Warm-up: built for one kayaker, but a common core for the squad, which takes longer to organise. And the six-to-twenty-four work-to-rest stays the same. The classic mistake is listing differences without causes.

So set a goal-specific aim first, plan safety as a process, and build the warm-up and cool-down for the setting, naming the cause of every difference. That frames the session, but the middle is still empty. Where do skill, conditioning and tactics go in a session?
